summary: This document describes integrating the Network Service Header (NSH) with Segment Routing to support Service Function Chaining, with encapsulation details. Segment Routing steers packets between service function forwarders along a path. NSH keeps the service plane, instance context, and metadata separate from transport.

eli5.summary: NSH is a folder describing which helpers a package must visit, and Segment Routing is the road plan. This shows how to use both without mixing them up.

questions: what is the network service header
subtitle: How the Network Service Header and Segment Routing can work together to steer traffic through chains of network services.

tldr.problem: Service Function Chaining needs both a service plane (which services, in what order, with what metadata) and a transport that steers packets between service forwarders, and the two need to coexist cleanly.
tldr.mechanism: Segment Routing (SR-MPLS or SRv6) carries packets between Service Function Forwarders while the Network Service Header keeps the service path and metadata. The SFF caches the SR information while the service function works on the packet, then reattaches it.
tldr.outcome: Operators can mix transports across their network and still have an end-to-end NSH service plane. IANA assigned IP protocol number 145 to the NSH and SRv6 endpoint behavior End.NSH.

today: RFC 9491 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2023. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it is the current specification of NSH integration with Segment Routing.

sections.title: Service Function Chaining and Its Rationale
sections.content:
Operators need to apply a service-derived forwarding policy to packets passing through Service Functions (SFs). Cascading SFs at the 3GPP Gi interface (N6 in 5G) showed three limits: redundant classification in many SFs, SFs receiving traffic they should not process (for example TCP proxies receiving UDP traffic), and complex, properly ordered invocation of several SFs.

Service Function Chaining (SFC, RFC 7665) decouples the service topology from the physical network. The IETF created a transport-independent encapsulation for it, the Network Service Header (NSH, RFC 8300), so that the SFC work does not have to be repeated for each transport.
sections.eli5: Some traffic must pass through helpers such as a filter or a cache, in the right order. SFC is the system for sending it through them without redoing the road network each time.

sections.title: SFC within Segment Routing Networks
sections.content:
RFC 8300 says how to carry the NSH directly in a link-layer header. This document adds IP protocol number 145 so the NSH can also sit directly inside an IP header.

Segment Routing (RFC 8402) steers a packet along an ordered list of instructions called segments. SR-MPLS and SRv6 can both encode an SF as a segment, but steering is only part of what SFC needs. Simplified classification at intermediate SFs and shared context (metadata) matter too.

The RFC describes two scenarios, each usable with either SR-MPLS or SRv6, and they can be combined. A classifier MUST use one NSH Service Path Identifier (SPI) for each SR policy, so different flows can share an SFP and different SR policies can coexist on it.
sections.eli5: Segment Routing is a list of stops written on the package. That alone does not tell the helpers what to do, so the NSH checklist is kept as well.

sections.title: Scenario One: NSH-Based SFC over an SR Transport
sections.content:
Here SR-MPLS or SRv6 is the transport between Service Function Forwarders (SFFs), and the NSH conveys and triggers SFC policy. The RFC's example uses SPI 100 and an initial Service Index (SI) of 255, with SFs in two data centers, DC1 and DC2.

After classification in DC1, packets are sent to SFF1 as an inner packet with NSH: SPI 100, SI 255. SFF1 uses the SPI and SI to hand the packet to SF1. SF1 applies its service and decrements the SI to 254. SFF1 looks up SPI 100, SI 254 and forwards to DC1-GW1. That gateway looks at the NSH and adds an SR encapsulation (SR-MPLS or SRv6) toward DC2-GW1. At DC2 the SR encapsulation is removed, SFF2 hands the packet to SF2, the SI drops to 253, and the lookup shows the end of the chain.

Benefits listed: the NSH's transport independence, SR traffic engineering where appropriate, and a clear division of responsibility between the NSH and SR.
sections.eli5: The package carries its checklist the whole way. Between faraway buildings it rides on a special delivery road, and each time a helper finishes, the number on the checklist counts down.

sections.title: Scenario Two: SR-Based SFC with an Integrated NSH Service Plane
sections.content:
Here the SFs are NSH-aware, so no SFC proxy should be needed. SR does SFF-to-SFF transport and the NSH keeps the service plane, the SFC context and any metadata. Each service hop is a segment in the SR segment list.

When a packet reaches an SF's segment, the SFF looks up the SID for that SF (a Prefix-SID in SR-MPLS, or the new END.NSH behavior in SRv6). The lookup yields next-hop context, such as the destination MAC address for Ethernet toward the SF. The SFF strips the SR information, updates it, and saves it in a cache indexed by the NSH SPI and the SI decremented by 1. When the SF returns the packet, the SFF finds the SR information using the SPI and SI, pushes it back on top of the NSH and forwards to the next segment.

If reclassification at the SF changed the SPI or SI to values not in the cache, the lookup fails and the SFF must generate an error and drop the packet.

The SF itself is unaware of SR. That lets SF vendors support a single unified SFC solution and removes the need for an SR proxy or reclassification in the SFF.
sections.eli5: The helper does not understand the road map. So the delivery person tucks the map into a drawer under the checklist's next number, hands the package to the helper, and pulls the map back out when the helper returns it.

sections.title: Packet Processing for SR-Based SFC
sections.content:
For SR-MPLS, when an SFF receives a packet destined to a local Prefix-SID associated with an SF, it strips the label stack, updates the SR information and saves it in the cache indexed by SPI and SI minus 1. That saved information is used to re-encapsulate packets coming back from the SF.

For SRv6, when a node receives a packet destined to a local End.NSH SID, processing follows RFC 8754 section 4.3.1.1 up through line S15. Then the node removes and stores the IPv6 and SRH headers in a local cache indexed by service-path-id, service-index - 1 (S15.1), and submits the packet to the NSH FIB lookup (S15.2). This interrupts normal SRH processing, which does not continue to S16 at that time. When the SF returns the packet, the node reattaches the cached headers using the NSH values and resumes from line S16.

The cache must remove entries at an appropriate time chosen by the implementation, which MAY be operator-configurable. If a packet from an SF has no matching cached entry, the SFF SHOULD log it and MUST drop the packet.
sections.eli5: The delivery person writes the route on a sticky note, files it under the package's checklist number, and pulls it back out to carry on. If no note matches, the package is thrown away and the problem is written down.

sections.title: Encapsulation with SR-MPLS and SRv6
sections.content:
With SR-MPLS the segment routing header is a stack of MPLS labels, followed by the NSH Base Header, Service Path Header and metadata. At the tail end of the label stack the NSH-based SFC has to terminate. This can use the NEXT operation, which needs an indication that the NSH follows the stack as in RFC 8596, or the CONTINUE operation, which equals MPLS Ultimate Hop Popping. For CONTINUE, the penultimate hop must not pop the top label and expose the NSH to the wrong SFF, which is done with the No Penultimate Hop Popping (No-PHP) flag in the Prefix-SID Sub-TLV. A dedicated Prefix-SID per node for this use is RECOMMENDED.

With SRv6 the packet carries the SRH (Next Header, Hdr Ext Len, Routing Type, Segments Left, Last Entry, Flags, Tag, a segment list of 128-bit IPv6 addresses, optional TLVs) followed by the NSH. The NSH is indicated by its IP protocol number in the Next Header of the SRH.
sections.eli5: The stack of labels is the outer wrapping and the NSH is the note inside. The tricky part is making sure the wrapping is only taken off at the right place, so that the note is not read by the wrong helper.

sections.title: Compatibility, Caching, MTU and Security
sections.content:
If an SRv6/IPv6 node does not recognize the NSH, it follows section 4 of RFC 8200. An SR-MPLS node follows section 3.18 of RFC 3031. Operators are RECOMMENDED to increase the underlying MTU so SR/NSH traffic crosses an SR domain without fragmentation.

The Security Considerations section adds nothing new. It points to RFC 7665 for SFC in general, to RFC 8300 for the NSH, and to RFC 8754 and RFC 8663 for segment routing.
sections.eli5: If a router does not understand the checklist it follows the usual rules for unknown things. Roads should be wide enough that the package with its extra wrapping is not squashed. Safety rules come from the earlier documents.
